title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
summary: A self-contained specification of the basic protocol for Internet electronic mail transport, SMTP. It covers how mail is handed from sender to server and between servers. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 5321.

plainLanguage.summary: SMTP is the postal service rules for email. It says how one computer hands a letter to another, who it is for, and what to do if the address is wrong.

questions: what do smtp reply codes mean
how does smtp find the mail server for a domain
subtitle: The self-contained rulebook for moving Internet email between servers: commands, replies, relaying and retries.

tldr.problem: Internet mail needs a reliable, efficient way to hand a message from a sender to a destination, possibly through several intermediate hosts, with clear rules about who is responsible for it.
tldr.mechanism: An SMTP client opens a channel to a server, sends MAIL, RCPT and DATA commands that name the sender, the recipients and the message, and the server answers each command with a numeric reply; the next hop is found with DNS MX records.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2821 consolidated RFC 821 and related documents, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 5321, which is the current SMTP specification.

today: RFC 2821 was a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 821, RFC 974 and RFC 1869. It has itself been obsoleted by RFC 5321 and was updated by RFC 5336. Use RFC 5321 for the current SMTP specification.

sections.title: What This Specification Is
sections.content:
The objective of the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) is to transfer mail reliably and efficiently. It needs only a reliable ordered data stream channel; this document describes transport over TCP. RFC 2821 is a self-contained specification that consolidates, updates and clarifies the original SMTP of RFC 821, the domain name system requirements for mail from RFC 974, mail transport material from RFC 1123, and the SMTP extension mechanism, without adding or changing existing functionality. Where it does differ from earlier documents, it supersedes them.

An important feature is the ability to carry mail across networks, called relaying. A message may pass through several intermediate relay or gateway hosts on its way from sender to final recipient. The Mail eXchanger mechanism of the domain name system identifies the next-hop destination.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the one big rulebook that says how email moves from computer to computer, gathering up older rules into one place.

sections.title: The Client, the Server and Extensions
sections.content:
When an SMTP client has a message to send, it opens a two-way channel to an SMTP server. The client sends commands and the server sends replies. The dialog is deliberately lock-step, one command at a time, although agreed extensions such as command pipelining can change this. A server may be the final destination, a relay (it then acts as a client toward the next server) or a gateway (it carries the message onward using a protocol other than SMTP).

Transfer can take one hop or a series of hops, but at each handoff the protocol requires that the server accept responsibility for either delivering the message or properly reporting the failure. When the same message goes to several recipients at the same destination, the protocol encourages sending only one copy of the data.

After the server's 220 greeting, the client normally sends EHLO, which both identifies the client and asks the server to list the service extensions it supports. Older systems, or clients that need no extensions, may use HELO, and the server MUST NOT return the extended response to HELO. A client should be able to fall back to HELO if the server does not recognize EHLO.
sections.plainLanguage: One computer calls another and they take turns, like a polite phone call. The one who takes the letter promises either to deliver it or to tell you it could not.

sections.title: The Mail Transaction
sections.content:
A mail transaction has three steps and the commands MUST be used in this order. MAIL FROM:<reverse-path> starts the transaction and names the sender mailbox, which is used to report errors. One or more RCPT TO:<forward-path> commands then name the recipients, one each. Finally DATA asks to send the message; the server answers 354 and treats the following lines as message text until a line containing only a period.

That final period also confirms the transaction, and the server answers 250 once it has stored the message. Message data MUST NOT be sent unless a 354 reply is received. Because a lone period ends the message, a client inserts an extra period at the start of any line that begins with one, and the server removes it; this is the transparency procedure.

Servers SHOULD NOT reject messages because of perceived defects in the message headers or body. Other commands include RSET, NOOP, QUIT, and VRFY and EXPN for checking an address or expanding a mailing list.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the post office who the letter is from, then who it is for, then hand over the letter, and finish by saying 'that is all'. If the letter itself has a line that says 'that is all', you add a small mark so it does not fool the clerk.

sections.title: Replies and Failure Handling
sections.content:
Every command generates exactly one reply: a three-digit code followed by text. A client MUST decide what to do from the code, not the text. The first digit says whether the command worked: 2yz is success, 3yz means more information is expected, 4yz is a temporary failure that may succeed if repeated, and 5yz is a permanent failure. A client MUST be prepared to handle unknown codes by interpreting the first digit only. Multiline replies put a hyphen after the code on every line except the last.

Examples include 220 service ready, 221 closing, 250 completed, 354 start mail input, 450 mailbox unavailable, 452 insufficient storage, 550 mailbox unavailable (including policy rejections), 552 exceeded storage allocation and 554 transaction failed.

If a server that accepted a message later finds it cannot be delivered, it MUST construct an undeliverable-mail notification to the sender. To avoid error loops, such a notification uses a null reverse-path, written MAIL FROM:<>, and servers MUST NOT send notifications about problems with notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply starts with a number that tells you at a glance if things went well, if you should try again later, or if you should give up. The words after the number are mostly for people.

sections.title: Finding the Next Hop, Relaying and Retries
sections.content:
To deliver to a domain, the client MUST do a DNS lookup, first looking for MX records. If there are none but an address record exists, it is treated as an implicit MX with preference 0. If MX records exist, address records MUST NOT be used unless they are located through those MX records. Lower preference numbers are tried first, and servers with equal preference MUST be randomized to spread load. The client MUST be able to try each address in the list until a delivery succeeds, and SHOULD try at least two.

Explicit source routes are discouraged: clients SHOULD NOT generate them, and servers MAY decline to accept them. A relay may accept or refuse the relaying task; if it declines for policy reasons it SHOULD return 550. A relay MUST NOT inspect or change the message headers or body except to add its own Received: line and, optionally, to detect loops.

Mail that cannot be sent right away MUST be queued and retried. The retry interval SHOULD be at least 30 minutes, and the give-up time generally needs to be at least 4 to 5 days. Clients MUST use timeouts on each command, for example 5 minutes for the initial 220 greeting and 10 minutes while waiting for the reply after the end of the message data.
sections.plainLanguage: To find where to send a letter, you look up the address of the town's mail office. If it is closed, you try again later, and keep trying for several days before telling the sender it did not work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that SMTP mail is inherently insecure: even casual users can talk directly to servers and create messages that appear to come from somewhere else. Mail cannot be authenticated, and integrity checks cannot be provided, at the transport level, so real security lies in end-to-end methods such as digital signatures on message bodies. It calls efforts to stop users from setting envelope return paths and From fields to other valid addresses largely misguided, because they break legitimate uses.

Sites may disable VRFY or EXPN for security reasons, but then the server MUST return a 252 reply rather than a code that could be mistaken for success or failure. EXPN has been used to harvest addresses for spammers, so sites should weigh the trade-offs. Servers may refuse mail for operational reasons, but the RFC urges care. Because open relaying has been used to hide the origin of mail, implementations SHOULD be able to limit relaying to known sources, rejecting with 550.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can write any return address on an envelope, so the post office cannot prove who sent a letter. If you really need proof, you sign the letter itself.
